articles.body:
**NEW YORK — In a press conference Thursday morning that began with routine remarks about tourism and ended in visible confusion, Mayor Mamdani announced that**

**Times Square will soon be officially renamed “New Red Square,” a move he repeatedly emphasized has “absolutely nothing to do with communism.”**

**“I just like red,” the mayor said, standing before a backdrop that had, for the occasion, been subtly adjusted to a deeper shade. “It’s a strong color. It’s bold. It’s energetic. New York is energetic. This is not complicated.”**

**The plan, which will take effect later this summer pending what aides described as “minimal logistical adjustments,” includes updated signage, rebranding efforts, and a coordinated push to “lean into red as a unifying visual theme.”**

**City officials stressed that the name change is purely aesthetic.**

**“People hear ‘Red Square’ and they jump to conclusions,” said one senior advisor. “This is about branding. This is about vibrancy. This is about a mayor who, frankly, prefers one color over others.”**

**Still, the announcement has prompted questions.**

**When asked directly whether the name carried any historical or ideological connotations, the mayor shook his head.**

**“No,” he said. “None. I have never been to the other one. I don’t think about the other one. This is a completely separate red square.”**

**Tourism officials appeared cautiously**

**optimistic, noting that Times Square has long thrived on spectacle and reinvention.**

**“If people want to come take photos in a place called New Red Square, they will,” said one representative. “They already come here to stand in the middle of traffic and look up.”**

**The rebranding effort is expected to include a shift in lighting design, with several major billboards reportedly agreeing to incorporate more red tones during peak hours. Early mockups depict the square bathed in a uniform crimson glow, which one planner described as “striking, possibly overwhelming, but definitely consistent.”**

**Local reaction has been mixed.**

**“I mean, it’s already a lot,” said one visitor from Ohio, glancing around the square. “I’m not sure making it redder is the issue we’re facing.”**

**Others expressed support, if only for the clarity.**

**“At least now it sounds like what it feels like,” said a street performer dressed as Spider-Man. “A little intense. A little aggressive. Kind of hard to leave.”**

**Back at City Hall, the mayor acknowledged that some residents might take time to adjust.**

**“Change is part of what makes New York**

**great,” he said. “Also, again, it’s just a color.”**

**He paused briefly before adding, “And it’s a very good one.**
articles.deck: Mayor Announces Plan to Rename Times Square ‘New Red Square,’ Insists It’s Just a Color Preference
articles.author: Mort Adella
articles.title: Mayor Announces Plan to Rename Times Square “New Red Square”, Insists it’s Just a Color Preference

articles.excerpt: A generation raised on screens has, against all advice, decided to dress like the cast of an oil painting about teething.
articles.body:
A generation raised on screens has, against all advice, decided to dress like the cast of an oil painting about teething.

The trend, which began in late winter on a single TikTok account belonging to a graduate student who has since deleted it, involves what proponents describe as “strategic infantilization” and what dermatologists describe as “concerning, please stop.”

## How it works

A proper BabyMaxx outfit requires, at minimum, one bonnet, two pairs of socks worn over jeans, a teething ring used as a bracelet, and what the community calls “a confused expression.” The look is finished with a small spoon.
articles.deck: Bonnets are back, allegedly on purpose.
articles.author: Iris Halloran
articles.title: Inside BabyMaxxing, fashion’s most unsettling new youth aesthetic

articles.excerpt: We tried four-day weeks. We tried summer Fridays. The data is in: Monday simply does not deliver value to shareholders.
articles.body:
We tried four-day weeks. We tried summer Fridays. The data is in: Monday simply does not deliver value to shareholders.

Monday, frankly, has been coasting on legacy goodwill for two centuries. Sunday is beloved. Friday is essential. Tuesday is functional. Monday is, at best, a placeholder.

This column proposes — modestly, in the long tradition of modest proposals — that we simply skip it. Stop scheduling it. Stop counting it. Let it lapse, like a magazine subscription nobody renewed.
articles.deck: It’s not a serious proposal, except in the ways that it is.
articles.author: Devin Royce
articles.title: Opinion: Maybe we should just cancel Monday and see what happens
